newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU BSE inquiry to vote on Commission censure.
newsitem.headline: EU BSE inquiry to vote on Commission censure.

text.p: A European Parliament committee of inquiry met on Wednesday to consider a threat to censure the European Commission for mishandling the mad cow crisis.

At the end of the first dasy of a two-day meeting, the 19-member cross-party committee had dealt with about half the 254 amendments to a report by Spanish Socialist Manuel Medina Ortega criticising the EU executive and Britain, where mad cow disease originated.
If agreed by the committee, the threat of censure action and the report as a whole will be put to the vote in the full parliament on February 19.

The proposal for a censure motion, which will be examined on Thursday, gives the Commission until December to take corrective measures sought by the parliament, including a reorganisation of EU veterinary services and a shake-up of advisory committees.

If not, the assembly would immediately call a vote on a censure motion which would force Commission President Jacques Santer and his 19 colleagues to resign if it gets the required two-thirds majority.
Santer told the inquiry in mid-January the Commission planned similar changes, due to be announced later this month.
The committee, which had earlier targeted senior EU officials alleging that they had mismanaged the crisis, appeared to have moderated its demands.
"We don't want to see heads roll. We want to see our demands go through," Friedrich Wilhelm Graefe zu Baringdorf, of the Green Group, told a news briefing.
The Greens, who proposed the censure threat, claimed the support of the parliament's two largest political groups -- the Socialists and Christian Democrats.
Parliamentary sources said little action would be taken against Britain, noting that any legal move would have to be made through the Commission.
British Socialist Philip Whitehead said he would vote against any amendment calling for financial compensation from Britain for losses caused by the mad cow crisis.
"The purpose of the inquiry is to ensure that a crisis like the BSE crisis never happens again - not to determine financial liability or carry out a witch-hunt," he said in a statement.

The draft report identified 13 points of alleged British negligence, including failure to enforce properly a ban on exports of animal feed containing infected meat and bone meal and urging Brussels to avoid inspecting British slaughterhouses between 1990-94.
The mad cow crisis hit the headlines in March 1996 when London admitted that the fatal cattle brain disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) could spread to humans who ate infected beef.
